title: Inequalities used in practice
dek: Markov, Chebyshev, Hoeffding, and Jensen are not trivia. They are how you bound a tail, justify a concentration inequality, or remember that means and transforms do not commute.
story: Graduate probability is full of inequalities that look like homework until you need a sample-size floor, a multiple-testing union bound, or a reason that E[log L] is not log E[L]. The ones that actually show up in a genomics lab are few, and they are worth keeping sharp.

Markov: for Y ≥ 0 and t > 0, P(Y ≥ t) ≤ E[Y]/t. Chebyshev is Markov applied to (Y − μ)²: P(|Y − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k². These bounds are often loose. Their job is existence and scaling — n in a denominator — not a pretty 95% interval.

Hoeffding-type bounds control tails of bounded independent sums and underwrite many “n log p” multiple-testing sample-size slogans. Jensen says that for convex φ, φ(E[Y]) ≤ E[φ(Y)]. Log-likelihoods, KL, and log-transforms of CFU all live or die on that convexity.
deepTitle: Four bounds, written so you can use them
deep: Union bound: P(∪ Aⱼ) ≤ ∑ P(Aⱼ). This is the Bonferroni calculation. For m tests each at level α/m, family-wise error ≤ α regardless of dependence. The price is power. FDR procedures refuse this bound as the operating criterion; they do not refute it as a probability inequality.

Hoeffding (bounded independent sum): if Yᵢ ∈ [aᵢ,bᵢ] independent, S = ∑ (Yᵢ − E[Yᵢ]), then P(S ≥ t) ≤ exp{−2t² / ∑ (bᵢ−aᵢ)²}. Binary DST calls are bounded. Read counts are not; do not quote Hoeffding on raw RNA-seq.

Jensen on the log: E[log Y] ≤ log E[Y] for Y > 0. The MLE maximises a sample average of log f; the ELBO in variational Bayes is a Jensen bound on log m(y). Confusing E[Y] with exp(E[log Y]) is how geometric-mean CFU slides lie.

Chebyshev gives a distribution-free 1/k² tail. For k = 3, at most 1/9 of the mass sits beyond 3σ. A Normal tail at 3σ is about 0.003. If you need the Normal tail, you have assumed a shape, not invoked Chebyshev.

formulas.label: Chebyshev
formulas.note: Distribution-free. Loose if you actually have light tails.

formulas.label: Jensen
formulas.note: Equality iff φ is linear on the support, or Y is degenerate.

visual.caption: How much tail you can claim from Chebyshev versus a Normal model at the same kσ. The bars are upper bounds or actual tail probabilities, not data. Chebyshev is honest and conservative; Normal is a shape assumption.

example.title: Union bound on 20 independent DST genes
example.setup: You flag a gene if a permutation p-value is < 0.05. There are m = 20 candidate genes. Under a global null, what does Bonferroni actually guarantee?

steps.title: Write the union
steps.body: Let Aⱼ be the event that gene j is flagged. Family-wise error is P(∪ Aⱼ). Without independence, the only free bound is ∑ P(Aⱼ).

steps.title: Set per-test α
steps.body: If each test is valid at level 0.05/20 = 0.0025, then FWER ≤ 20 × 0.0025 = 0.05. That holds even if genes are in LD.

steps.title: Name the cost
steps.body: A true resistance gene with modest n will often fail 0.0025. FDR (next plates) spends the error budget on the expected fraction of false discoveries among rejections, which is a different operating characteristic — not a tighter union bound.

example.takeaway: Use Markov/Chebyshev/union when you need a guarantee without a shape. Buy a shape (Normal, permutation) when you need power.

check.prompt: Jensen’s inequality implies that for CFU counts Y > 0:
choices: log(E[Y]) ≥ E[log Y], so the log of the mean is at least the mean of the logs
The MLE of E[Y] is exp(mean log Y)
check.answer: log(E[Y]) ≥ E[log Y], so the log of the mean is at least the mean of the logs
check.why: log is concave, so the inequality reverses relative to the convex statement: E[log Y] ≤ log E[Y]. Geometric means sit below arithmetic means.

whyWrong.The MLE of E[Y] is exp(mean log Y): That would be a lognormal-mean estimator, not a general MLE of E[Y].

check.prompt: Using only Chebyshev, a distribution-free bound on P(|Y−μ| ≥ 2σ) is:
check.why: 1/k² with k = 2 is 1/4. The Normal tail ~0.05 is a different, stronger assumption.

whyWrong.≤ 0.05: That is a Normal-ish tail, not Chebyshev.
whyWrong.≤ 0.003: That is a Normal 3σ tail, misplaced.
whyWrong.= 0: Chebyshev never claims a zero tail at finite k.

check.prompt: On the small-multiples plate, why is the Chebyshev bar always taller?
check.figureHint: Panels for k = 2, 3, 4 with Cheb vs Normal.
choices: Because Chebyshev assumes lighter tails than Normal
Because Chebyshev is a distribution-free upper bound, while the Normal bar is a specific tail probability
Because kσ is defined only for Chebyshev
check.answer: Because Chebyshev is a distribution-free upper bound, while the Normal bar is a specific tail probability
check.why: The plate is a reminder that a bound is not a tail. You may use the bound when you refuse a shape.

whyWrong.Because Chebyshev assumes lighter tails: It assumes almost nothing; that is why it is larger.
